title: Access & Equity Lens
subtitle: Not a separate program and not a separate group of students — a lens you apply to every tool so each student reaches grade-level mathematics and sees themselves as capable.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: NCTM, Principles to Actions — Access & Equity (2014) · Ladson-Billings & Gay (culturally relevant/responsive pedagogy) · CAST, Universal Design for Learning · Cohen & Lotan (assigning competence / complex instruction).

blocks.text: What it is
A way of looking at every routine and every lesson and asking: *Does every student have a genuine way into this mathematics, and does every student leave seeing themselves as a math person?*

It is woven into each tool in this toolbelt — every page has an *Access & Equity* section — and gathered here so the through-line is clear. The core stance is **asset-based**: instead of “these kids can’t do grade-level math,” we assume **every student can engage in rich mathematics with the right access**, and our job is to build that access. High expectations *and* high support — never one without the other.

blocks.title: Why this is a lens, not a tool

blocks.text: Equity isn’t a strategy you do on Tuesdays. It’s the question you carry into every routine. That’s why it has no single “how-to” — instead it shapes how you run a Number Talk, choose a task, pose a question, and decide who gets heard. It serves multilingual learners, students with IEPs/504s, and students who’ve struggled — and it raises the ceiling for *everyone*.
Four dimensions

rows: Can every student *enter* the mathematics? Is there a genuine way in regardless of reading level, language, or prior gaps?
Does every student get to be a *doer* of mathematics whose ideas matter — not just a receiver?
Are we holding the grade-level bar for all students, supporting them up to it rather than lowering it?
Do we honor students’ languages, backgrounds, and the many valid ways they were taught to do mathematics?

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: Access & equity in action
items: Tasks with a low floor and a high ceiling — everyone starts, no one tops out
Many strategies valued, including methods from home or other countries
Participation distributed; quiet and emerging-English students heard
Grade-level mathematics for every student, with scaffolds
Students positioned by name as capable (“Jordan’s strategy…”)

no.title: What equity is *not*
items: Lowering the bar or handing out easier “below-level” work
Pulling struggling students out of the rich task to drill
Only the confident, fluent-English students talking
“Being nice” in place of real mathematical challenge
One right method, taught one way, for everyone

blocks.text: The most common equity mistake is **lowering expectations out of kindness** — giving students who struggle less-demanding math “so they can succeed.” It feels supportive and it widens gaps. The equity move is the opposite: **keep the rigor, add the support.** Be a “warm demander” — high challenge, high care.
A handful of moves do most of the work, and they show up in every tool’s equity section:

items: **Low-floor / high-ceiling tasks** — a genuine entry point for everyone.
**Turn-and-talk + sentence stems** — rehearsal and language support.
**Wait time** — shifts participation from “fastest” to “everyone.”
**Multiple representations** — visuals, manipulatives, diagrams, not just symbols.
**Valuing multiple strategies** — including students’ home methods.
**Assigning competence** — publicly naming students’ mathematical strengths.

sections.label: Lesson design connection
sections.sources: Sources: NCTM Access & Equity (2014) · Cohen & Lotan, Designing Groupwork (assigning competence) · CAST, Universal Design for Learning · Gay, Culturally Responsive Teaching.

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson
Everywhere. The lens shapes the task you choose, the questions you pose, who you call on, and how you respond — in every component, starting with the opener.

You don’t run “an equity activity.” You run a Number Talk, an Error Analysis, a Same But Different — and the lens decides whether *every* student got into it. The most powerful access move happens before the lesson, in the numbers and task you pick.
A four-question planning check
Run any opener through these before you teach it:

items: **Entry:** Can every student start this in the first 30 seconds? (If not, lower the floor — friendlier numbers, a visual, an estimate first.)
**Language:** Where will multilingual learners rehearse and get words? (Plan the turn-and-talk and the sentence stems.)
**Participation:** How will I hear from more than the usual few? (Wait time, cold-call students I primed during turn-and-talk, record by name.)
**Rigor:** Am I keeping the grade-level math for everyone, adding support rather than removing challenge?

blocks.text: The moves, by student need

rows: Turn-and-talk before whole group; posted sentence stems; visuals and gestures; allow thinking/jotting in a home language; revoice to model academic language without correcting the idea away.
Reduce reading and working-memory load; record thinking publicly so it isn’t held in the head; manipulatives and visuals; extra wait time and no speed pressure; multiple entry points.
Low-floor tasks so they start with success; assign competence publicly (“watch what ___ noticed”); keep them *in* the rich task with support — don’t reroute them to drill.
Invite and honor methods from home or other countries; use contexts that reflect students; position students as knowers whose strategies teach the class.

blocks.text: Publicly and specifically name a student’s mathematical strength, especially a student with low status: *“Maria’s strategy of using a benchmark is something we should all try.”* It is genuine (not empty praise), it raises that student’s standing with peers, and it tells the class that **many ways of thinking are valued here** — which is the heart of disposition.

blocks.title: This is already in the vision

blocks.text: Our vision says *every* math classroom develops all five strands for students — the word “every” is the equity commitment. The lens is how we keep that promise honest: not “most kids reasoned today,” but *did this student, and that one, and that one?*
A quick equity self-check (after the lesson)

yes.title: Signs the lens is working
items: Students who rarely speak contributed
More than one method was honored
No one was quietly given easier math
A struggling student left with a success

no.title: Signs to adjust tomorrow
items: The same confident few carried the talk
MLLs stayed silent (add turn-and-talk / stems)
Some students never found an entry point
“Support” had quietly become lowered expectations

blocks.text: Where this leads

The same lens carries into **Core Instruction** and beyond — choosing low-floor high-ceiling tasks, sequencing student work so many voices are honored in the consolidation, and keeping grade-level rigor for every learner. Master it in the opener, where the stakes are low and the routine is short, and it becomes second nature everywhere else.
